topics: MMA is a round-based combat sport where current Unified Rules scoring prioritizes damaging/effective legal striking and effective grappling results over activity volume or static control.
Professional Unified Rules rounds are five minutes with one minute rest; bouts may be scheduled from one to five rounds and cannot exceed five rounds or 25 minutes.
The referee is the sole in-bout authority to stop a contest; doctor, corner, and referee stoppages affect official result pathways.
Three judges use the 10-point must system unless a promotion or amateur rule set specifies otherwise.
Effective striking is judged by the damage/effect of legal strikes; effective grappling is judged by impactful results from takedowns, submission attempts, reversals, and advantageous positions.
Effective aggressiveness and fighting-area control are tie-breakers only when effective striking/grappling does not separate the round.
10-9 indicates a close round win; 10-8 requires a large margin involving damage with dominance and/or duration; 10-7 indicates complete domination where stoppage is warranted.
Static control is not enough: dominant grappling must lead toward damage, submissions, positional advancement, or sustained effective offense.
Current Unified Rules prohibit knees or kicks to the head of a grounded opponent; grounded means any body part other than hands or feet touches the canvas.

Key fouls include headbutts, eye gouging, biting/spitting, hair pulling, fish hooking, spikes onto head/neck, strikes to spine/back of head, throat attacks, outstretched fingers toward eyes, groin attacks, stomping grounded opponents, fence/glove/shorts grabbing for control, small joint manipulation, attacks after bell or on break, and corner interference.
Rules can vary by jurisdiction, amateur federation, and promotion; backend output must confirm rule set before allowing borderline techniques.
Tag scoring lessons by damage, dominance, duration, effective_grappling, aggressiveness, and area_control.
Do not equate volume statistics with round-winning impact.
Generate rules-aware constraints for grounded opponent, fence work, submissions, and amateur-pro distinctions.
Surface local-rule verification whenever user mentions competition, sparring under event rules, or promotion-specific preparation.
MMA phases shift between open-space striking, clinch/fence, takedown transition, ground control, submission threat, ground striking, scramble, referee reset, and corner rest.

topics: MMA stance is an adaptive base for punches, kicks, clinch entries, takedown defense, and exits. It is usually less bladed than pure boxing and less square/static than traditional Muay Thai, with hands ready for striking, framing, underhooks, and defense.
Feet shoulder-width or slightly wider with rear heel light, knees soft, hips able to sprawl, check, pivot, or kick.
Hands protect chin and temples while avoiding extended fingers toward the opponent's eyes.
Lead hand manages range, hand-fights, frames, posts, and jabs; rear hand protects and fires straight counters.
Guard changes by range: long guard or frame outside, high guard/parry at boxing range, collar tie/frame in clinch, underhook/sprawl readiness near takedown range.
Stance must reset after every strike so the athlete can defend the next punch, kick, shot, or clinch.
MMA boxing entries must cross kicking, punching, clinch, and takedown danger. Reliable entries combine feint, jab, level-change cue, angle step, guard return, and planned exit or tie-up.
Enter behind information: feint, jab, touch, hand fight, low kick threat, or level-change cue before committing.
Move the head off center on rear-hand entries and do not finish square with feet trapped.
Use short combinations that end with exit, angle, clinch, or takedown threat rather than long static boxing flurries.
Blend strike-to-grapple and grapple-to-strike: punch into underhook, jab to level change, failed shot to hook, break from clinch to elbow or cross.
Match entry to range: jab/teep from long, double jab or cross from mid, hook/uppercut/elbow at close, knee/elbow from clinch control.

MMA kicking uses low kicks, calf kicks, body kicks, teeps, switch kicks, high kicks, and occasional spinning kicks, but every kick must account for catches, counters, stance recovery, and takedown exposure.
Set up kicks with hands, feints, stance movement, or opponent reactions; naked kicks are easier to catch or counter.
Turn the hip and standing foot for round kicks while keeping the non-kicking hand responsible for counters.
Return the kicking leg to stance quickly; a beautiful kick that leaves the athlete square is a poor MMA kick.
Low kicks are highest value when timed as the opponent steps, loads, retreats, or posts weight on the lead leg.
High kicks and spinning attacks require stronger gates: balance, flexibility, range reading, recovery, and ruleset-safe partner constraints.

sport_profiles.planning_summary: MMA combines striking, wrestling, clinch/cage control, ground control, submissions, ground-and-pound, transitions, fight IQ, contact management, and round-based conditioning. Training must connect phases and gate contact by domain readiness.
training_priorities: domain-specific level assessment instead of one global MMA label
stance, guard, range, and defense before contact escalation
cage wrestling, wall-walks, pummeling, and mat-return logic
ground position, posture, tap culture, and escapes before high-risk submissions
aerobic base, repeat-power conditioning, rotational power, trunk/neck/shoulder durability
contact load, symptoms, sleep, stress, and recovery tracked in athlete_state
fight-camp and opponent-specific work only for advanced, ready athletes

advanced.sparring: periodized by camp phase and readiness

common_injury_or_load_risks: neck overload from contact and grappling
shoulder, elbow, and wrist stress from posting, frames, pummeling, and submissions
rib and trunk irritation from clinch and body shots
knee, ankle, and adductor strain from kicks, shots, sprawls, and scrambles
fatigue and dehydration risk from unsafe weight cutting
do_not_pair: hard sparring with heavy neck work
hard live wrestling with heavy lower-body strength on poor readiness days
advanced submissions with beginner tap culture
late-camp novelty with high contact load
progression_guardrails: progress solo mechanics to cooperative partner work to constrained resistance to controlled sparring
use the weakest safety-relevant domain to gate contact and advanced drills
track contact load and symptoms like training load
reduce contact and live grappling when head, neck, joint, sleep, stress, or readiness signals are poor
